topic: The Elastic Collision Paradox: Counting Pi with Colliding Blocks
target_audience: High school students with an interest in physics and computer science

sections.title: The Setup: A Curious Mechanical System
lecture_lines: Two blocks on a frictionless surface.
Small block sits between wall and large block.
Elastic collisions conserve energy and momentum.
Collisions begin as the large block approaches.
This creates a rapid ping-pong effect.
animations: Create two circles with radius #FFFFFF, labeled C1 and C2.
Place a [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/block.svg] of mass m1 on the left side of C1.
Animate mass m1 moving towards a stationary mass m2.
Show the collision point between m1 and m2 using red color #FF0000.
Fade out [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/wall.svg] and m2 to represent the end of the initial state.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Conservation Laws
lecture_lines: Elastic collisions preserve total energy.
Both kinetic energy and momentum are conserved.
Blocks trade velocities based on mass ratios.
animations: Display Energy E = 1/2 m v^2 in light blue #ADD8E6 using [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/blocks.svg].
Display Momentum p = m v in light green #90EE90.
Show energy and momentum conserved with flashing indicator #FFFF00 using [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/blocks.svg].

sections.title: The Mathematical Mapping: Collision Count as Digits
lecture_lines: Mass ratios link collisions to digits of Pi.
Ratio 1 to 1 gives 3 collisions.
Ratio 1 to 100 gives 31 collisions.
Ratio 1 to 10,000 gives 314 collisions.
The number of collisions encodes Pi's digits.
animations: Show a series of collisions using [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/blocks.svg] to create digit-like patterns.
Label the collision count with Pi expansion digits using white #FFFFFF.
Highlight each new collision digit appearing with bold yellow #FFFF00.

sections.title: Visualizing the 'Phase Space' Geometry
lecture_lines: Collisions trace a circular arc.
Velocities map to coordinates in 2D.
Geometry explains why Pi appears here.
animations: Display phase space trajectory as a continuous arc.
Map trajectory segments to the circle's curvature in cyan #00FFFF.
Animate the point traveling along the arc using MoveAlongPath.
Show the arc length proportional to the mass ratio's square root.
Emphasize the intersection point with a white circle marker #FFFFFF.

sections.title: Conclusion: Why Pi Appears Everywhere
lecture_lines: Pi defines rotation and circular motion.
Constrained systems inherently produce Pi.
Our collisions are simply rotating in space.
Data from collisions forms a perfect circle.
Pi is fundamental to all oscillatory motion.
animations: Show the scaling factor sqrt(m1/m2) clearly in green #00FF00.
Conclude with the appearance of Pi as a fundamental constant in white #FFFFFF.
